How Much Peptide to Inject? Start With Your Prescribed Dose

Use a dose provided by your licensed healthcare professional; this calculator does not determine how much peptide you should inject (read why). You need three numbers from your vial label and your plan. The tool handles the unit conversions, so you never have to move a decimal point by hand.

  1. Enter the vial amount. This is the total peptide printed on the label, usually in mg (for example 5 mg or 10 mg). Use the mcg option if the label lists micrograms.
  2. Enter the water you added. Type the millilitres of bacteriostatic water used to reconstitute the powder. More water means a weaker solution and more units per dose.
  3. Enter your dose. Type the amount prescribed or planned for one injection, in mcg or mg.
  4. Pick your syringe. The calculator warns you if the draw does not fit, or if it is too small to measure well.
  5. Read the result. The large number is how many units to pull on the syringe. The drawing shows roughly where the plunger should sit.

Have not mixed the vial yet? Plan the water first with the peptide reconstitution calculator, a reverse peptide calculator that works backwards from the units you want to draw.

Peptide Calculator in Units: The Formula

The arithmetic takes three steps. Knowing it lets you double-check any result on paper.

1. Peptide concentration

concentration (mg/mL) = peptide in vial (mg) ÷ water added (mL)

2. Peptide volume per dose

volume (mL) = dose (mg) ÷ concentration (mg/mL)

3. Peptide dose in syringe units

units = volume (mL) × 100

The factor of 100 comes from the U-100 insulin syringe: one millilitre is divided into 100 units, so each unit holds 0.01 mL. It is the standard syringe for small subcutaneous volumes, and the one this page assumes.

Peptide Calculator Conversion Rules: mg, mcg, IU and Units

Four different things get mixed up on a vial label. Keep them separate and the peptide calculator arithmetic stays simple:

ConversionRuleWhat it means
mg to mcg1 mg = 1,000 mcgMass. Multiply by 1,000, divide to go back.
mL to syringe units1 mL = 100 units (U-100)Volume. One unit is 0.01 mL, whatever the vial contains.
Dose to unitsunits = dose ÷ concentration × 100Needs the mg/mL concentration from vial mg ÷ water mL.
IU to mgNo universal factorIU measures biological activity; the mg equivalent is specific to each product and its label.

A worked example ties the rules together: 5 mg in 2 mL is 2.5 mg/mL; 250 mcg is 0.25 mg; 0.25 mg ÷ 2.5 mg/mL = 0.1 mL; 0.1 mL × 100 = 10 units. The mg-to-mcg step changes mass, the mL-to-units step changes volume, and the concentration is the bridge between them. IU cannot be bridged without the product's own IU-per-mg figure printed on the label — if both the vial and the dose are written in IU, enter IU for both in the calculator above.

Syringe Calculator Peptide Example: 5 mg Vial

Say you have a 5 mg vial, you add 2 mL of bacteriostatic water, and your dose is 250 mcg. Here is the working:

  • Concentration: 5 mg ÷ 2 mL = 2.5 mg/mL, which is 2,500 mcg per mL.
  • Volume: 0.25 mg ÷ 2.5 mg/mL = 0.10 mL.
  • Units: 0.10 mL × 100 = 10 units on a U-100 syringe.
  • Doses per vial: 5 mg ÷ 0.25 mg = 20 doses.

If you had added 1 mL instead, the same 250 mcg dose would be 5 units. Less water gives a stronger solution and a smaller draw. With 3 mL it would be 15 units. The peptide dose is identical in all three cases — only the volume changes.

Peptide Calculator in Units: Syringe Chart

Units are a volume mark on the syringe, not a measure of peptide. Ten units always means 0.10 mL, whatever is in the vial. That is why the concentration matters: the same 10 units can hold 250 mcg in one vial and 500 mcg in another. For a refresher on handling an insulin syringe, MedlinePlus has a clear guide to giving an insulin injection.

Syringe sizes: 30, 50 and 100 units, or 3 mL

Every U-100 insulin syringe uses the same scale, so the peptide calculator result applies to all of them. Pick the smallest barrel that holds your draw; finer lines mean a more accurate dose.

SyringeHoldsSmallest lineBest for
0.3 mL insulin30 units1 unit (some ½ unit)Draws under 30 units
0.5 mL insulin50 units1 unitDraws of 30–50 units
1 mL insulin100 units2 unitsDraws of 50–100 units
3 mL standard3 mL (no unit marks)0.1 mLMeasuring bacteriostatic water, not doses

A 3 mL syringe is marked in mL, so divide the units by 100 to read it (20 units = 0.2 mL). Its 0.1 mL lines are too coarse for most peptide doses but ideal for adding water to a vial.

Peptide Calculator IU vs Syringe Units

Syringe "units" and IU (international units) sound alike but measure different things. Syringe units are volume: 100 units is 1 mL on a U-100 syringe. IU measure biological activity, and the conversion to mg is different for every substance, so there is no universal mg-to-IU factor.

If your vial is labelled in IU, select IU for both the vial and the dose in the peptide calculator above; mixing IU with mg is blocked because it needs the product's own IU-per-mg figure. Do not convert IU to mg with a generic factor — use the figure printed on the product label.

How to Reconstitute a Peptide Vial

The math above assumes you have already turned the freeze-dried powder into a solution. A consistent mixing routine keeps every draw from the same vial at the concentration you calculated:

  1. Wipe both stoppers. Swab the top of the peptide vial and the bacteriostatic water vial with a fresh alcohol wipe and let them air-dry for a few seconds.
  2. Draw the water. Pull air into the syringe equal to the mL of bacteriostatic water you are adding, inject it into the water vial, then draw the water out.
  3. Inject along the wall. Push the needle through the peptide vial stopper and angle it so the water runs slowly down the inside glass. Do not squirt directly onto the powder — it can foam and degrade.
  4. Dissolve gently. Roll the vial between your palms or swirl it slowly until the powder is fully clear. Never shake; foaming breaks peptide bonds.
  5. Label the vial. Write the concentration in mg/mL and the date you mixed it, so every later draw uses the same figure.

If you have not chosen a water volume yet, the peptide reconstitution calculator works backwards from a target number of units to the exact mL of water to add.

Pre-mixed or compounded liquid vials. Some suppliers ship semaglutide, tirzepatide and other peptides already dissolved, with a concentration printed in mg/mL on the label. For these you do not add water: enter the total mg of peptide in the vial and the total mL of liquid as the "water" figure. The concentration and units result come out the same way. If you only know the mg/mL and the volume, the peptide concentration calculator converts between mg/mL, mcg per unit and molarity directly.

Storage and Shelf Life

  • Unmixed powder. Store in the refrigerator (2–8 °C) or freezer, away from light. Most lyophilized peptides remain stable for months to years when sealed.
  • Mixed solution. Refrigerate at 2–8 °C after reconstituting. A reconstituted peptide is typically stable for 4–8 weeks; check the manufacturer's data sheet for the compound you are using.
  • Bacteriostatic water. Once opened, bacteriostatic water stays usable for about 28 days because its 0.9% benzyl alcohol preservative stops bacterial growth. Preservative-free sterile water is for single use only and should not be used for multi-dose vials.
  • Do not freeze the mixed solution unless the data sheet says otherwise — freezing can damage reconstituted peptides.

Bacteriostatic Water vs Sterile Water

Both are sterile, but only one is designed for a vial you will draw from more than once:

Bacteriostatic waterSterile water (preservative-free)
Preservative0.9% benzyl alcoholNone
Multi-dose vialsYesNo — single use only
Opened shelf lifeAbout 28 days refrigeratedUse immediately or discard
Best forReconstituting peptides for multiple drawsOne-time injections or IV use

Benzyl alcohol does not kill bacteria — it stops them reproducing — which is why a single vial of bacteriostatic water can be accessed many times safely. Use preservative-free sterile water only for a one-time draw, not for a peptide vial you will return to over weeks.

Peptide Calculator Accuracy Tips

The math is exact, but the draw is only as good as the inputs. A few habits keep results meaningful in practice:

  • Aim for 5–50 units per dose. Draws under 2–3 units are hard to read. If your result is tiny, add more water when you next reconstitute.
  • Match the syringe to the draw. A 0.3 mL syringe has 1-unit lines, so small doses are easier to measure than on a 1 mL barrel.
  • Write the concentration on the vial. Once mixed, label the vial with mg/mL so you never have to remember how much water went in.
  • Re-check the label. Some vials state total content per vial and others per pack. Enter the amount in the vial you are actually using.

Planning a weekly schedule? The peptide dosage calculator adds dosing frequency and shows how many days a vial will last.

Peptide Calculator by Body Weight: mg per kg

Some plans express a dose per kilogram rather than a fixed amount. The arithmetic is one multiplication: dose (mg) = dose (mg/kg) × body weight (kg). For example, 0.1 mg/kg at 80 kg is 8 mg. For a dose written in mcg/kg, do the same multiplication and divide the result by 1,000 to get mg.

Once you have that absolute dose, enter it with your vial strength and water volume in the peptide dosage calculator. It returns the U-100 units, doses per vial and days of supply. This is arithmetic only; whether a weight-based dose is appropriate, and which figure to use, is a decision for your prescriber.

Peptide Calculator FAQ

How does a peptide calculator convert mg to units?

It divides the vial's mg by the water added to get mg per mL, divides your dose by that concentration to get mL, then multiplies by 100 because a U-100 syringe has 100 units per mL.

Is this peptide calculator free?

Yes. It is free, needs no account, and runs entirely in your browser, so the numbers you enter are never sent to a server.

Does more water change the peptide dose?

No. Water only changes the concentration. With more water you draw more units for the same peptide dose; with less water you draw fewer units.

Can the peptide calculator handle blends?

Yes, if you calculate one component at a time. Enter that component's mg in the vial and its dose; the units you get also deliver the other components in the same ratio as the blend. The peptide blend calculator shows every component at once.

Does the peptide calculator work with IU?

Yes. Choose IU for both the vial amount and the dose; syringe units are still volume, so the result is the same arithmetic. For an IU vial, use the IU-per-mg figure on the product label if you need the mg equivalent.

Which syringe does the peptide calculator assume?

A U-100 insulin syringe, where 1 mL equals 100 units. The 0.3 mL, 0.5 mL and 1 mL barrels all use this same U-100 scale, so the unit result is identical whichever one you pick; only the barrel size and tick spacing change. If you use a 3 mL standard syringe marked in millilitres rather than units, divide the unit result by 100 to read it in mL (for example, 20 units = 0.2 mL).

Is a peptides calculator the same as a dosage calculator?

They use the same formula. A peptides calculator usually focuses on units per injection, while a dosage calculator also adds frequency and vial supply.

Is this a unit calculator for peptides?

Yes. It is a unit calculator for peptides in the practical sense: you give the vial, the water and the dose, and it returns the U-100 syringe units. For unit conversions with no dose involved, such as mg to mL or mcg to mg, the mg to mL calculator is the quicker tool.

This peptide calculator performs arithmetic only and is provided for educational purposes. It does not recommend any peptide, dose or protocol.
